script.intro: Hello, and welcome. In most companies, the attacker's goal is Domain Admins, the group that controls every Windows computer and account. They rarely get there with a single trick. They walk there, one permission at a time. Today you'll follow that walk from a helpdesk account to the top.

steps.say: The setting. Nimbus Analytics in Hyderabad, Tuesday the tenth of November 2026. All times are UTC. A helpdesk worker, h.verma, fell for a phishing email, so the attacker has that account's password. The case folder has the company's identity data: which accounts are in which groups, and what each group is allowed to do.

Switch sides and think like the attacker. In the identity tool, open the Attack paths tab, start from h.verma, and ask for paths to Domain-Admins. Each arrow is one thing the attacker can do with what they already have.
steps.after: Let's read the path, hop by hop. h.verma is a member of Helpdesk. Helpdesk has ForceChangePassword on svc-sql, a service account, because of reset rights on the Service Accounts folder, inherited since 2023. That hop needs no new password: the attacker simply sets a new one. svc-sql is a member of Server-Admins. Server-Admins is admin on app02. Now the important one: adm.k.nair has a session on app02. A scheduled task called Nightly KPI export runs as adm.k.nair with a saved password, so that login sits on app02 every night. Anyone who is admin on app02 can take those credentials. And adm.k.nair is a member of Domain-Admins. So: phished helpdesk account, reset a service account's password, admin on a server, take the saved Domain Admin login. Game over. Notice that t.mehta and n.ali, the other Server-Admins members, could walk the same path from Server-Admins onwards. So which single change breaks the most paths? Removing the saved Domain Admin login from app02, by running that task as a low-privilege account, breaks every path that goes through it. Removing the old helpdesk reset right closes the door at the start. Do both. Answer the questions: svc-sql, and app02.

steps.say: That was one step from Seminar 7, Identity from both sides: AD, Entra and cloud IAM. The full seminar has a longer video, every step at three levels, walkthrough, practice and solo, a graded hand-in that I mark myself, and a certificate at the end. The links are on your screen. If you want to try the Hacker Room, the analyst desktop where all these programs live together, the free trial is linked there too.

script.outro: To recap. Attackers think in graphs, not lists. Each hop is something normal on its own: a group membership, an old permission, a saved login. Put them together and they lead to the top. Defenders win by finding the hops that many paths share, and removing them. Thank you for watching.

# Free tutorial: One group membership to domain admin

Follow an attack path from a helpdesk account to Domain Admins, one relationship at a time.

The files for this seminar are in `~/case` (Linux) and `case/` (Python): `captured/app02-sync-ps1.txt`, `captured/zeek-kerberos.log`, `cloud/audit.json`, `cloud/policies.json`, `eventlogs/app02-Security.jsonl`, `eventlogs/dc01-Security.jsonl`, `identity/ad_edges.csv`, `identity/users.csv`, `README.txt`.

## 1. The setting

This free tutorial is one step from **Seminar 7: Identity from both sides: AD, Entra and cloud IAM**. Follow an attack path from a helpdesk account to Domain Admins, one relationship at a time.

> Nimbus Analytics, Hyderabad. Tuesday 10 November 2026. All times UTC (India is UTC+5:30).

The evidence is in `~/case`. Read the README there if you want the whole story.

## 2. Walk it like an attacker

Now switch sides. In the **Attack paths** tab, start from h.verma (the phished account) and ask for paths to Domain-Admins. Each arrow is one thing the attacker can do with what they already have.
